analysis.one_liner: Raises car and truck fuel economy to 35 mpg, caps power plant pollution, and repeals oil industry tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The comprehensive energy and climate bill introduced in June 2007 by Sens. Collins and Lieberman was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised fuel economy requirements for cars and light trucks to at least 35 miles per gallon by model year 2019 and 45 by 2030, closing the loophole that let SUVs and light trucks meet a weaker standard. It would have required fuel providers to cut the greenhouse gas emissions of transportation fuel, capped sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury from power plants, extended tax credits for renewable electricity, funded weatherization to cut home heating and electric bills, and repealed two oil industry tax breaks. The Senate never acted on it; it sat in the Finance Committee until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households: drivers get lower gasoline bills from higher fuel economy standards, onboard fuel economy displays, fuel-efficient tire standards, and a removed cap on the tax credit for hybrid cars; low-income households get weatherization assistance to cut heating and electric bills; everyone breathing air near power plants benefits from mandated cuts in mercury, smog, and acid rain pollutants; and the public gains research and standards aimed at reducing petroleum use and climate-changing emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, homeowners, and communities near power plants

how_it_helps.text: Requires a combined average fuel economy standard of at least 35 miles per gallon for cars and light trucks beginning in model year 2019 and 45 miles per gallon by 2030, and bars regulators from treating SUVs and light trucks differently from cars after model year 2013, effectively ending the SUV loophole.

Requires the EPA to make each fuel provider cut the average lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of its transportation fuel by 5 percent below the baseline by 2015 and 10 percent by 2020, and expands the renewable fuel requirement to 35 billion gallons by 2025 with strict definitions of qualifying renewable biomass.
Caps sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury emissions from electric generation facilities under the Clean Power Act title.

Extends tax credits for renewable electricity production and residential energy efficient property, funds weatherization assistance, and creates an efficiency resource standard for retail electricity and natural gas suppliers, aimed at lowering heating and electric bills.

Repeals oil industry tax provisions covering the amortization of geological and geophysical expenditures and the depletion allowance for oil and gas wells, ending two subsidies to major integrated oil companies.

Removes the cap on the number of hybrid and advanced-lean-burn vehicles eligible for the consumer tax credit and adds a manufacturing credit of up to roughly $1 billion per year for companies retooling to build fuel-efficient vehicles.

Creates a national tire fuel economy program with minimum fuel economy standards for replacement tires, onboard fuel economy displays and tire-pressure alerts in new vehicles, and fuel economy standards for heavy-duty trucks and work trucks.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies lose two tax breaks and face a low-carbon fuel standard; coal-heavy electric utilities face mandatory cuts in sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury; automakers must meet steadily rising fuel economy targets; and taxpayers fund the vehicle manufacturing credits, renewable electricity credits, weatherization, transit corridors, and research programs. Consumers could face somewhat higher new-vehicle prices in the near term before fuel savings accumulate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies, coal-heavy utilities, and automakers

drawbacks.text: The bill ramps the renewable fuel mandate to 35 billion gallons by 2025 and expands the small ethanol producer credit for sucrose and cellulosic ethanol, and it builds in an elaborate process to study and mitigate 'adverse lifecycle impacts' such as water pollution, deforestation, and effects on food and feed prices — an acknowledgment that pushing this much biofuel into the market carries real environmental and food-price risks.

Rising fuel economy standards tend to raise the upfront price of new vehicles, a cost that falls hardest on buyers who keep cars a short time or cannot afford a new car, and the bill relies heavily on regulator discretion, letting the Transportation Secretary set final standards at levels other than the 35 and 45 mpg targets.

The vehicle manufacturing credit, idling reduction credit, renewable electricity credits, and transit corridor grants are all taxpayer-funded subsidies, and the $1 billion annual allocation for manufacturers is channeled through the automakers themselves rather than directly to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — higher fuel economy, lower power plant pollution, home weatherization, and repeal of oil tax breaks — would deliver savings and health benefits to ordinary households that outweigh its costs over time, and much of its fuel economy framework later became law in another bill that same Congress. Its weakest point is the ethanol expansion: the bill itself anticipates potential harm to food prices, water, and forests and builds a mitigation bureaucracy to manage it, so the biofuel title is a costly giveaway with uncertain public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a markup or vote until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Susan Collins introduced the Energy Independence, Clean Air, and Climate Security Act of 2007 on June 6, 2007, together with Sen. Joseph Lieberman.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
No further action — no committee markup, no subcommittee action, no floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies kept their tax breaks and faced no low-carbon fuel standard, coal-heavy utilities faced no cap on sulfur, mercury, or carbon dioxide, and automakers stayed under the weaker existing fuel economy rules for the remainder of the 110th Congress.

for.name: Sen. Susan M. Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Joined Collins in introducing the bill in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 6, 2007 and took no further action — no markup or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party breakdown exists; the bill's sole recorded sponsors were a Maine Republican and an Independent from Connecticut.

industries.note: The bill repeals the oil industry's amortization of geological and geophysical expenditures and the oil and gas depletion allowance, and obligates fuel providers to cut the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of their fuel. The industry's interest in keeping those subsidies and selling high-carbon fuel runs against the public's interest in lower fuel costs and cleaner air.

The Clean Power Act title requires regulators to cut sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury from electric generation facilities, the pollutants that drive acid rain, smog, and mercury contamination. The industry's cost is the public's health gain, though some utilities also gain from the extended renewable electricity credits.

The bill mandates rising renewable fuel volumes reaching 35 billion gallons by 2025 and expands the small ethanol producer credit, guaranteeing a growing market for biofuels. It entrenches the industry while the bill's own study process flags possible water pollution, deforestation, and food-price effects, so the industry's gain and the public's benefit do not fully align.

Automakers face sharply higher fuel economy targets, but the bill pairs them with a manufacturing tax credit of up to $1 billion a year for retooling, an R&D credit for efficiency components, and repeal of the cap on the consumer hybrid credit that expands the market for efficient vehicles. On the whole the industry is helped to comply rather than just penalized.

The bill creates minimum fuel economy standards and testing and labeling requirements for replacement tires. Compliance costs are modest but real; the benefit is lower fuel bills for every driver who buys tires.

The bill extends the renewable electricity production credit and the residential energy efficient property credit and creates an efficiency resource standard for electricity and natural gas suppliers, expanding the market for wind, solar, and efficiency services. The industry's growth here tracks the public's interest in lower bills and cleaner power.
